name: South Sea Company

summary.text: The South Sea Company was a British chartered company that in 1720 won a parliamentary scheme to convert a large part of the national debt into its own shares. Its share price rose and collapsed in 1720. A House of Commons Committee of Secrecy sat behind closed doors from February to June 1721 and reported on the company's directors and on ministers who had received stock; the company's cashier Robert Knight fled abroad with its ledger, Chancellor of the Exchequer John Aislabie was found guilty by the Commons and expelled, and Parliament confiscated the directors' estates. The 1720 Bubble Act required new joint-stock companies to be incorporated by royal charter.

facts.claim: Under the 1720 scheme Parliament enabled the South Sea Company to take on about £31.5 million of unconsolidated government debt in exchange for its shares, with the government paying 5 percent interest on the converted debt.
facts.quote: the company took on about an additional £31.5 million in unconsolidated government debt in exchange for shares, with the government paying 5 percent interest on the converted debt.

facts.claim: In January 1721 the company's cashier Robert Knight fled England with the company ledger known as the Green Book, which held the names of those implicated in the scheme.
facts.quote: In January 1721, Knight fled with the South Sea Company's ledger known as the Green Book, which held the names of those implicated in the South Sea Company scheme.

facts.claim: In January 1721 an Act of Parliament forbade the South Sea directors from leaving England or serving as directors of the Bank of England, the East India Company or the South Sea Company.
facts.quote: In January 1721, an act of Parliament forbade directors of the South Sea Company from leaving England or serving as directors in the Bank of England, East India Company, or South Sea Company.

facts.claim: A University of Southampton discussion paper states that the Committee of Secrecy discovered £574,000 of stock option bribes given to members of Parliament to pass pro-South Sea legislation. The Cornfield Gazette's figure of £574,500 was not found in the sources consulted.
facts.quote: The committee discovered the £574,000 of stock option bribes given members of Parliaments to pass pro-South Sea legislation.

connections.claim: John Blunt, a founder of the South Sea Company who sold out early, testified to the 1721 Committee of Secrecy with the names of those implicated, in exchange for leniency.
connections.quote: John Blunt, a founder of the company who cashed out early, testified to the committee with the names of those implicated in the South Sea Bubble in exchange for leniency.

connections.claim: As Chancellor of the Exchequer, John Aislabie negotiated the 1720 agreement between the Government and the South Sea Company, led the effort to persuade the Commons to accept it, and introduced the bill in April 1720. In 1721 a Commons committee accused him of speculating heavily in South Sea stock before the Act passed, and an Act declared him incapable of sitting in Parliament or holding office.
connections.quote: As Chancellor of the Exchequer, John Aislabie negotiated the agreement between the Government and the South Sea Company which led to the South Sea bubble, took the leading part in persuading the House of Commons to accept it, and introduced the bill giving effect to it in April 1720.

openQuestions: The site's figure of £574,500 in fictitious stock to ministers and MPs: the Southampton paper gives £574,000; the exact sum should be checked against the Committee of Secrecy reports (Harvard CURIOSity digitised copy; Parliamentary Archives HL/PO/JO/10/2/157).

Harvard's page says Aislabie was 'expelled from the House of Lords'; History of Parliament treats him as a Commons member declared incapable of sitting. The Tower of London imprisonment was not confirmed in the sources consulted.

The site's claim that the Bubble Act 'secured an exclusive monopoly for London elite banks' is an interpretation not stated by the sources; sources describe it as requiring royal charters for new joint-stock companies.
The site lists 'King George I & Royal Mistresses' as insiders; no source consulted addressed this.
Whether Robert Knight ended in the Austrian Netherlands (Harvard) or France/Paris (History of Parliament) is unresolved between the sources.
